title: Is the mind more than the brain?
realQuestion:
A neuroscientist can tell you which region lights up when you see red, which lesion takes your speech, which drug flattens your mood. None of that is disputed by anyone in this argument, and the page is not about it.

What is disputed is whether that story, completed, would be the whole story. When you see red there is something it is like to be you at that moment — the [[qualia]] of the experience. The question is whether a complete physical description of your brain would have described that, or would have left it out — and if it left it out, what follows.

The two sides are not neuroscience against religion. They are two answers to a question neuroscience does not ask.

distinctions.label: Does the mind depend on the brain?
distinctions.gloss: Yes, and nobody arguing here denies it. Damage the brain and you damage the mind, reliably and specifically. Every position on this page has to accommodate that, and each says how. Set aside, and covered in the note below.

distinctions.label: Would a complete physical account of the brain be a complete account of the mind?
distinctions.gloss: This is the argument on this page. It is a question about explanation and about what exists, not about which brain regions do what.

distinctions.label: Does anything survive death?
distinctions.gloss: A further step. Even a soul, if there is one, might not be the kind of thing that outlasts a body without help. The step from dualism to survival is a theological argument, not this one, and is not attempted here.

glossary.definition: The felt quality of an experience — what red looks like from inside, rather than which wavelength it is. Whether this names a real further thing is much of the dispute.
The view that a person is made of two things, a body and a soul, which interact. Distinct from the weaker claim that mental properties are not physical properties.
The principle that every physical event has a sufficient physical cause. Not a discovery so much as a working assumption of physics, which is part of why it is arguable.
David Chalmers' name for the question of why physical processing is accompanied by experience at all, as distinct from the tractable questions of how the brain discriminates, integrates and reports.

sides.label: The subject of experience is not one more thing in the brain

arguments.claim: A complete inventory of your body would not yet have said which person you are
arguments.explanation:
Richard Swinburne's argument turns on a question physical description seems unable to settle. Take a full specification of a body and brain — every atom, every connection. Now ask whether the person in it is you. Swinburne argues that this remains an open question after all the physical facts are in, and that a question that stays open after every physical fact is settled must be about something further.

He is not denying that the soul depends on the brain, and he is explicit that it does. The claim is about what a person is, not about whether minds can float free of bodies.

quote.text: a person consists of two parts — a physical body and a non-physical soul
quote.author: Richard Swinburne
quote.locator: the thesis defended at length in The Evolution of the Soul (1986)

counter.objection: The open question may be about our concepts rather than about the world. That we can ask 'but would it be me?' shows something about the elasticity of personal-identity talk, not that there is an extra ingredient the question is tracking. We can ask 'but would it be the same ship?' about a rebuilt vessel without anyone concluding that ships have souls. And an [[substance dualism]] that grants full dependence on the brain has to say what the soul is contributing that the brain is not already doing.
counter.response: The ship case is not parallel: there is no fact about which the ship's own answer could be right or wrong, and about yourself there is. Either you wake up tomorrow or someone else does, and that is not a matter of how we choose to speak.

variants.label: Hylomorphism
variants.heldBy: Thomas Aquinas and the Thomist tradition; Edward Feser, Eleonore Stump, David Oderberg
variants.oneLine: The soul is not a second thing joined to a body but the form of the body — what makes this matter a living human at all.
variants.summary:
The older Christian account, and the one Aquinas actually held. It is not Descartes with different vocabulary: on this view a human being is one substance, not two, and the soul is what a living body's organisation *is* rather than a passenger inside it.

That is why the interaction problem does not arise in the usual form — there are not two things to interact. What the tradition adds, and what makes it dualist at all, is that this particular form is subsistent: unlike the form of a tree, it can persist when the matter it organises is gone.

quote.text: the soul is the substantial form of the living human body … and it is unique among the forms of material things in being subsistent, that is, capable of surviving beyond the death of the body
quote.author: Edward Feser

variants.changesTheObjection: The objection above is that the open question — 'but would it be me?' — shows something about the elasticity of our concepts rather than about the world. This position never ran that argument. It reaches the soul from a general account of what any substance is, not from an intuition about personal identity, so a diagnosis of that intuition leaves it untouched.

objection.text: A form that can survive the matter it is the form of is not obviously coherent: a form is supposed to be the organisation of something, and an organisation with nothing organised is hard to distinguish from the second substance the view says it is not. Critics inside the tradition and outside it both press this, and the usual reply — that the intellect's operations are immaterial and so the form that performs them can subsist — depends on an argument about abstraction that few philosophers outside Thomism accept.
objection.response: A subsistent form in separation is admitted to be in an unnatural state, which is why the tradition insists on bodily resurrection rather than treating the disembodied soul as the person.

variants.label: Christian materialism
variants.heldBy: Kevin Corcoran, Nancey Murphy, Peter van Inwagen, Trenton Merricks
variants.oneLine: There is no soul. A human person is a material thing, and the Christian hope is bodily resurrection, which is what it always said.
variants.summary:
This position is on the theist side of the page and agrees with the atheist side about the metaphysics. Its argument is partly exegetical — that the Bible's anthropology is unified rather than Platonic, and that its hope is resurrection rather than the immortality of the soul — and partly philosophical: the soul was imported from Greek philosophy and has been doing damage since.

Corcoran's version has persons constituted by their bodies without being identical to them, on the model of a statue and the bronze: the same relation, not the same thing.

quote.text: we human persons are constituted by our bodies without being identical with the bodies that constitute us
quote.author: Kevin J. Corcoran
quote.work: Rethinking Human Nature: A Christian Materialist Alternative to the Soul

variants.changesTheObjection: Nothing in the objection above is aimed at anything this holds. It agrees that the open question is a fact about concepts, agrees there is no further ingredient, and would agree with most of the atheist side of this page — which is the point of printing it, because a reader who takes dualism to be the Christian position is wrong about a growing minority of Christian philosophers of mind.

objection.text: If a person is a material thing, the resurrection has an identity problem the soul was invented to solve: the atoms disperse, and a being assembled later from other matter looks like a very good copy rather than you. The constitution relation also does the work of a distinction without the metaphysics of one — saying you are constituted by your body but not identical with it either means there are two things after all, or means nothing that survives being pressed.
objection.sharedPremise: it argues from premises this position holds — that God exists, that the resurrection is bodily, and that a person must be numerically the same person afterwards — to the conclusion that a purely material account leaves nothing to carry that identity across the gap.
objection.response: Numerical identity across a gap is a problem for any account that takes the resurrection to be bodily, including dualist ones, since the dualist also needs the raised body to be yours. Van Inwagen and Merricks have offered answers; none is comfortable, and none is worse than a soul nobody can locate.

arguments.claim: If consciousness cannot be reduced, a universe that starts with mind explains it better than one that does not
arguments.explanation:
This argument does not begin with the soul. It begins by granting the hardest version of the problem to the other side and asking which picture of the world accommodates it.

On a naturalist account, mind appears late, out of arrangements of matter that were never mental, by a route nobody can specify — and its appearance is either a brute fact or a very long promissory note. On theism, mind is where the universe starts, and finite minds are the kind of thing such a universe would be expected to contain. J.P. Moreland's argument is comparative and conditional: it does not claim to prove consciousness irreducible, only that if it is, this counts.

quote.text: If irreducible consciousness exists (or is regularly correlated with physical states), then this provides evidence (to a degree specified in chapter two) for God's existence.
quote.author: J.P. Moreland
quote.work: Consciousness and the Existence of God: A Theistic Argument
quote.locator: the conditional the book sets out to defend

counter.objection: The conditional is doing less than it appears, because the antecedent is the whole dispute and the consequent smuggles in a comparison never run. 'Mind is fundamental' explains consciousness the way 'it is in the nature of opium to cause sleep' explains sleep: it re-describes the thing at a higher price. A divine mind is itself an irreducible consciousness, unexplained, so the account ends where it started with one more entity in it.
counter.response: Every explanation stops somewhere, and stopping at mind is not obviously worse than stopping at matter. The claim is only that if consciousness is not reducible, a universe with mind at the bottom is less surprised by it.

sides.label: Mind is what brains do, and nothing has been left out

arguments.claim: Every mental capacity we have located has turned out to be a brain function
arguments.explanation:
The positive case is a two-century record with no counterexample. Every capacity once thought too inward to be physical — memory, language, recognising a face, moral judgement, the sense of being a self — has, when investigated, turned out to be something specific neural tissue does, and to fail in specific ways when that tissue fails.

Patricia Churchland's point is that this is not a series of correlations awaiting a deeper explanation. It is what finding out what something is looks like. Nobody now says water is correlated with H₂O.

quote.text: When I say that the mind is the brain, when I say that vision just is a function of the brain, that's what I mean … that there is nothing other than the cells and the way they're put together.
quote.author: Patricia Churchland
quote.locator: spoken; a false start has been elided

counter.objection: The strongest form of this objection comes from within naturalism rather than from religion. David Chalmers accepts every result Churchland cites, denies souls, and still argues that the list is a list of functions — discriminating, integrating, reporting — and that explaining a function does not explain why performing it is accompanied by experience. Water and H₂O is the wrong parallel, because there is nothing it is like to be water: the identity there needs no further fact, and here one is exactly what is in dispute.
counter.sharedPremise: it accepts naturalism and every neuroscientific result cited, and argues from those premises that explaining what a system does is not yet explaining why doing it is accompanied by experience.
counter.response: The 'further fact' may be an artefact of the first-person view rather than a further thing in the world. A system that models itself will represent its own states as simple and immediate, and will find their explanation in functional terms unsatisfying, whether or not anything has been left out.

variants.label: Illusionism
variants.heldBy: Keith Frankish; Daniel Dennett; Jay Garfield
variants.oneLine: There is no hard problem because there is nothing of the kind it is about: introspection misrepresents our experiences as having phenomenal properties they do not have.
variants.summary:
The most radical position on this side, and the one that takes the hard problem most seriously by refusing its starting point. Illusionists do not deny that we are conscious; they deny that consciousness consists in private qualities of the kind the debate assumes.

What needs explaining, on this account, is not why physical processing is accompanied by experience but why we are so sure it is — and that is a question about how a self-modelling system represents its own states, which is hard but not of a different kind from other problems in cognitive science.

quote.text: phenomenal consciousness … is an introspective illusion — introspection misrepresents experiences as having phenomenal properties
quote.author: Keith Frankish
quote.work: Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness, Journal of Consciousness Studies 23

variants.changesTheObjection: The objection above says that explaining a function does not explain why performing it is accompanied by experience. This position denies the thing the 'why' is asking about: there is no accompaniment, only a system that represents itself as having one. The objection cannot be pressed without assuming exactly what is in dispute.

objection.text: An illusion is a way things seem, and seeming is the thing in question — so the position appears to presuppose what it denies. Chalmers calls this the hardest of the hard cases and its defenders concede the shape of the problem: to say experience is an illusion is to say there seems to be experience, and it is not clear what that could be if not experience. The reply, that seemings can be cashed out in purely informational terms, is precisely what critics say has never been done.
objection.sharedPremise: it accepts naturalism and the entire functional story about what brains do, and argues from those premises alone that an account which explains a seeming by calling it a misrepresentation still owes an account of the seeming.
objection.response: It has been attempted rather than assumed: an informational state that represents a state of the system as simple and intrinsic is a seeming, and building one is an engineering problem rather than a metaphysical one.

variants.label: Panpsychism
variants.heldBy: Philip Goff, Galen Strawson, Luke Roelofs; a growing minority in philosophy of mind
variants.oneLine: Consciousness is not produced by brains at all: it is a basic feature of matter, and brains organise it rather than create it.
variants.summary:
This position accepts the hard problem in full and concludes that the mistake was made at the start. Physics describes what matter does, not what it is; the intrinsic nature of matter is left blank, and consciousness is a candidate for filling it. On that account experience does not have to be got out of the non-experiential, because there is no non-experiential to get it out of.

It is emphatically not a religious view — Goff, Strawson and Roelofs are not theists — which is why it is on this side of the page. It is also not the fringe position it sounds like: the argument is that it is the only view which is both realist about consciousness and free of the emergence problem.

quote.text: consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of the physical world
quote.author: Philip Goff
quote.work: Galileo’s Error: Foundations for a New Science of Consciousness

variants.changesTheObjection: The objection above asks why physical processing should be accompanied by experience. On this view the question has a presupposition it rejects — that the physical was ever experience-free — so there is no accompanying to explain. The objection has to be reformulated as a question about combination instead, which is a different and much more specific difficulty.

objection.text: The combination problem, and it is severe. Even granting that electrons have some minimal experience, nothing explains how billions of tiny subjects add up to one subject reading this sentence — and a sum of experiences is not obviously an experience at all, any more than a crowd of people is a person. Critics argue the view has relocated the hard problem rather than solved it, exchanging 'how does experience arise from the non-experiential' for 'how do micro-experiences compose', with no more traction on the second.
objection.response: The combination problem is at least a problem about how things of one kind make a thing of the same kind, which is the ordinary business of science. Emergence of experience from the wholly non-experiential is a change of category, and that is the harder ask.

arguments.claim: A soul that moves a body would have to displace a physical cause that is already sufficient
arguments.explanation:
This is the argument that has done the most work in the last forty years, and it is aimed at dualism's action rather than at its plausibility. Physics appears to obey [[causal closure]]: for any physical event, there is a sufficient physical cause. Your arm rises because of muscle fibres, motor neurons, and a chain running back into the brain, with no gap.

Jaegwon Kim's exclusion principle then bites. If the soul also caused the arm to rise, the event has two sufficient causes, which is either overdetermination — a coincidence repeated every time anyone moves — or one of the two causes is not doing anything. Kim pressed this against fellow physicalists first, which is part of why it is hard to dismiss as prejudice.

quote.text: No single event can have more than one sufficient cause occurring at any given time — unless it is a genuine case of causal overdetermination.
quote.author: Jaegwon Kim
quote.locator: the causal exclusion principle, as stated in the supervenience argument

counter.objection: Kim aimed the argument at fellow physicalists before he aimed it at anyone else, and its sharpest critics are physicalists too. Stephen Yablo, Karen Bennett and the causal-compatibilist literature argue that the exclusion principle misdescribes causation across levels: a determinable and its determinate are not two competing sufficient causes, and neither are a mental state and its physical realiser, so nothing is being overdetermined and nothing has to be idle. Kim himself takes the argument to show that irreducible mental properties are causally inert, a conclusion many naturalists find as unacceptable as any dualist does. Causal closure is also an assumption of physical practice rather than a result of it: no experiment has surveyed all the causes of an event and found them all physical.
counter.response: That the closure principle is not a theorem is granted. It is, however, the best-supported working assumption in the sciences, and nothing has ever been found to violate it — while the alternative requires an interaction with no mechanism, no location and no energy budget.
counter.sharedPremise: it accepts physicalism and the causal closure of the physical, and argues from those premises alone that the exclusion principle misdescribes how causes at different levels relate, so that a mental cause and its physical realiser are not two candidates competing for one job.

notes.heading: The argument that was withdrawn by the man who made it
notes.text:
For twenty years the sharpest anti-physicalist argument was Frank Jackson's: Mary knows every physical fact about colour vision but has never seen colour; when she is let out of her black-and-white room, she learns something; so not every fact is a physical fact.

Jackson then changed his mind and became a physicalist, concluding that Mary's surprise does not show what he had taken it to show. That is why the argument is here rather than in one of the slots above: it is a famous argument its own author abandoned, and a page that spent a slot on it would be showing an argument nobody in the current dispute is pressing in that form. It matters anyway — a philosopher publicly reversing a career-defining position is rare enough to be worth knowing about, and both sides now cite the reversal for opposite reasons.

notes.heading: What both sides agree the brain does
notes.text:
Dualists on this page are not disputing the neuroscience, and it is worth being exact about that because the argument is usually misreported as if they were.

Swinburne holds that the soul's every conscious state depends on the brain in this life, so that anaesthetic, injury and dementia do exactly what they appear to do. Moreland's argument does not require dualism at all, only that consciousness resist reduction. Neither position predicts that a lesion will leave a capacity intact, and neither is embarrassed by a scan. The disagreement is about what a complete physical story would and would not have contained, and no scan settles that.

whereItStands:
The empirical trend runs one way and has for a long time. Capacities keep turning out to be brain functions, and no mental phenomenon has ever been localised outside the head. Anyone arguing that the mind is more than the brain is arguing against that current, and the honest ones say so.

The philosophical dispute has not moved with it. [[the hard problem]] is roughly where Chalmers left it in 1995: nobody has produced a derivation of experience from physical description, and nobody has produced an argument that no such derivation is possible which the other side accepts. What has changed is the shape of the field — the live options are now mostly forms of physicalism and forms of naturalistic non-physicalism, with theistic dualism a minority position argued by a small number of philosophers who argue it well.

That last fact cuts less than it looks. A position held by few can be right, and the reason to attend to Swinburne is that his argument is good, not that many share his conclusion.
commonMistake:
Christians most often argue as though the neuroscience were the opponent, and reach for cases — near-death reports, terminal lucidity — that would be striking if they held up and that no serious version of the argument needs. The strong version concedes the dependence entirely and asks a question the dependence does not answer. Reaching for anomalies makes a philosophical claim look like a factual bet, and it is losing bets that have made dualism sound disreputable.

Atheists most often treat a correlation as a conclusion. That a region lights up when you feel fear tells you where fear happens; the claim in dispute is that the lighting-up is what the fear is, which is a further claim and one that Chalmers, an atheist, spends a book denying. Producing more scans does not address it.

The shared error is thinking the other side must be ignoring evidence. Neither is. They are disagreeing about what would count as having explained something.
